A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ChatHuman and provide readable main texts, equations, tables, figures, references, and appendices. The title and organization change substantially, but corresponding methods and experiments can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original ChatHuman experiments on tool usage, pose estimation and generation, body measurements, and human-object interaction, including ablations and supplementary evaluations.

after.justification: v2 retains original ChatHuman results and adds video-generation comparisons, tool-composition evaluations, additional agent comparisons, and repeated tool-holdout experiments.

M1.justification: v2 introduces query-dependent prediction and execution of node, chain, and directed acyclic tool graphs, supported by generated multi-tool instructions (Sections 3.2 and 9.9). It also adds video-generation tools. These extend the procedure beyond v1's retrieval, existing composite tools, and result integration; motion generation and capture already appeared in v1's appendix.

E1.justification: v2 adds demonstrated video-generation and character-animation tasks and evaluation of queries requiring longer tool compositions. The established image, pose, contact, and measurement datasets remain. Motion-generation examples and multi-turn dialogue evaluation were already present in v1's appendix and are not new coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds GPT4Tools-FT and Visual ChatGPT-4 to the 3DPW/RPE pose comparisons (Table 13), where they were absent in v1. It also evaluates a GPT-4 replacement for ChatHuman's agent (Table 10) and adds a qualitative video comparison with Pika (Figure 8). Existing principal comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: New evaluations train with at most three-tool graphs and test combinations up to five tools, partition 26 tools into nine folds, and vary held-out coverage across three, five, and seven tools. The added pose-agent comparison specifies a T-pose fallback for failed calls. These are additional protocols, not evidence that the retained benchmark experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of longer-than-training tool compositions, sensitivity to the number and selection of unseen tools, and replacement of the LLaVA agent with GPT-4. Existing paper-component, retrieval-embedding, integration, and multi-turn analyses remain. Conversely, v1's dedicated failure-case examples and unsupported-task analysis are removed.

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-trial reporting. v2 reports three randomized tool-holdout trials and their mean in Table 14, and averages the GPT-4-agent comparison over three repeats. This introduces limited repeated-evaluation reporting, without confidence intervals, standard deviations, or specified random seeds.

E6.justification: Matched existing benchmark scores are largely unchanged. Added results include RPE MPJPE values of 190.5, 168.4, and 147.2 for GPT4Tools-FT, Visual ChatGPT-4, and ChatHuman, respectively (v2 Table 13), plus composition, holdout, and GPT-4-agent results. Main measurement tables omit baseline weight errors; ChatHuman's weight result remains in supplementary Table 17.

T1.justification: Neither version introduces theoretical guarantees or proofs. The retrieval, transformation, and evaluation mathematics is retained or re-expressed. Separating tool-call and response cross-entropies in v2 explicates the textual supervision categories already trained in v1; the graph mechanism is described procedurally rather than through new formal analysis.

C1.justification: The central claims about paper-based retrieval, tool-result integration and discrimination, and strong task performance remain. v2 expands the claimed capabilities to explicit graph-based invocation and video animation. Its stronger emphasis on chatting does not establish a wholly new contribution, since user interaction was already central to v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of robustness to longer compositions and varying unseen-tool sets, and explicitly identifies dependence on the quality of available academic tools. It removes v1's discussion of incorrectly answering unsupported requests and its video-generation limitation. Limitations involving vague requests and inaccurate height labels remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds LangChain parsing/invocation details and the tool-graph generation prompt. It changes a promised release into stated availability of code, models, and data, with licensing restrictions described in Section 8. Most hyperparameters and hardware details remain. Table 11 introduces an inconsistency: 26 tools with three instructions each still totals 66 instructions.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially into motion/video generation and tool documentation and composition, including CHAMP, Stable Video Diffusion, EasyTool, ToolPlanner, and TaskBench. v2 explicitly situates its approach against documentation-assisted and multi-tool agents. Several earlier application, action-recognition, and orthogonal-finetuning citations are removed; these changes exceed bibliographic updating.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and substantial method and related-work prose are rewritten. Model training becomes a separate subsection, dataset descriptions are redistributed, and the appendix is reorganized into numbered method, evaluation, ethics, and results sections with a contents list. This is extensive editorial restructuring beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The paper switches from single-column to two-column presentation and extensively reorganizes displays. v2 revises the opening illustration, adds graph, integration, discrimination, and animation diagrams, moves the tool inventory into the main text, merges comparison tables, and adds experimental tables. Weight columns and dedicated failure-case illustrations are removed.

improvement.justification: The added pose-agent comparisons and tool-holdout/composition tests strengthen empirical support for ChatHuman, while the new diagrams clarify its operation. The gain is qualified: video evidence remains qualitative, baseline weight comparisons and dedicated unsupported-task failure analysis are removed, and the revised data-generation prompt contains an inconsistent instruction count. Overall, v2 provides useful but limited quality improvements beyond its expanded scope.
